definition.text: The study of how humans interact with the pedosphere and with key parts of the biosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

facts.text: It is one of the general subfields of edaphology, alongside agricultural soil science, and studies human interaction with the pedosphere beyond crop production.

Its topics include surface water quality, vadose zone functions, septic drain fields, wastewater land treatment, stormwater, erosion control, contamination and remediation, wetland restoration, soil degradation and nutrient management.
It also covers movement of viruses and bacteria in soil, bioremediation, microbes engineered to degrade pollutants, land use, global warming, acid rain and anthropogenic soils such as terra preta.
Much of the research in environmental soil science is done with models.
Soil chemistry's emphasis has shifted toward environmental soil science, whose knowledge is key to predicting the fate of contaminants in soil.

definition.text: The relation between two overlapping terms: soil quality, a soil's fitness for a given purpose, and soil health, a holistic view of soil as a self-sustaining living system.

facts.text: Soil health has largely replaced the older term soil quality, though the two still overlap considerably.
Soil quality meant fitness for a use, such as quality of soil for maize production or for roadbed preparation.
The phrase soil health comes from European organic or biological farming movements, well before soil quality became a discipline around 1990.
Swiss soil biologist Otto Buess's 1978 essay 'The Health of Soil and Plants' largely defines the field even today.

title: Interpretations of soil health

definition.text: The differing ways users define soil health, understood as a soil's condition at a defined place and scale against benchmarks of healthy functioning.

facts.text: Because users weigh a soil's functions differently, the term only makes sense in the context of the user's aims and the boundary of the soil in question.
Ecological landscape assessment and agronomic objectives give potentially conflicting interpretations, each claiming its own criteria; a soil can function well ecologically yet not serve crops.

Benchmarks differ with a soil's inherited qualities and geography; generically, a healthy soil absorbs and cycles well, sheds clean runoff, keeps carbon and productivity near climatic limits and leaks few nutrients.
Unlike soil quality, soil health is not applied to a purpose such as preparing a roadbed.

contested_note: Sources describe many potentially conflicting interpretations, especially ecological landscape assessment versus agronomic objectives.

title: Soil health testing

definition.text: Assessing soil health by measuring the ecosystem services a soil provides against benchmarks, combining physical, chemical and biological analyses.

facts.text: Benchmarks used include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium.
Testing is spreading in the United States, Australia and South Africa; Cornell University has had a Soil Health Test since 2006, and Woods End Laboratories a soil quality package since 1985.
Both combine aggregate stability, mineral balance and CO2 respiration analyses, now considered hallmarks of soil health testing.
Other labs add biological factors to routine chemical nutrient tests, notably a soil respiration test called the CO2-Burst.
Many labs and scientists resist new biological tests because fertility metrics rest on crop-response models that do not exist for soil health; critics say novel tests may miss management changes.
Over the past 40 years US soils may have lost up to 75% of their carbon (humus), though how much is debatable; critics say old testing models have failed.
Older models stressed maximum yield, while nutrient pollution of US surface and groundwater grew, reported in the early 2000s as the worst since the 1970s.
In practice soil health testing tends to be confined largely to agronomic objectives.

contested_note: Sources report resistance among labs and scientists to new biological tests and call the extent of US soil carbon loss debatable.

definition.text: A concept, introduced by Maharjan and colleagues in 2020, that uses native land in a region as the benchmark for measuring how far managed soils fall short in health.

facts.text: Soil's importance for food security, agro-ecosystems, the environment and human life has shifted research strongly toward soil health.
Without site- or region-specific benchmarks, research on how different agronomic management affects soil health had been limited.

definition.text: The chemical, physical and biological measurements used to judge soil quality, since soil function itself cannot easily be measured directly.

facts.text: Physical indicators measure texture, bulk density, porosity, water content at saturation, aggregate stability and penetration resistance, showing infiltration and water available to plants.
Chemical indicators include pH and nutrient levels; a typical soil test evaluates only chemical properties.
Biological indicators reflect organisms such as earthworms, millipedes, centipedes, ants and spiders, which regulate soil structure, degrade contaminants and cycle nutrients.
Soil quality can be evaluated with the Soil Management Assessment Framework, and in Germany agricultural soil quality is rated on the soil value scale (Bodenwertzahl).
Very few monitoring systems give near real-time indicator data, and almost all of them report only at research level.

title: Soil as a filter and buffer

definition.text: The soil's role in regulating water and in filtering, buffering and transforming materials that move between the atmosphere, plant cover and water table.

facts.text: Soil particles capture contaminants, so water comes out cleaner in aquifers and rivers.
Soil transforms and decomposes waste materials into new materials.
It can store large amounts of carbon as soil organic matter, lowering atmospheric carbon dioxide and helping mitigate climate change.

title: Mapping soil functions

definition.text: Mapping soil properties as interpretations for particular functions, such as food production, environmental protection or civil engineering.

facts.text: Soil mapping identifies, describes and delineates soil types from field observation or from inferences drawn from sources such as aerial photographs.
Maps can show single properties, such as critical nutrient or heavy-metal levels, or combined interpretations such as an erosion risk index.
It extends soil survey, using maps of soil components with pedotransfer functions and soil inference models to infer how mapping units will perform.

distinct_from: Soil as a filter and buffer

definition.text: The ability of a soil to resist destabilising influences or recover its healthy state after them.

facts.text: It is a subset of the broader notion of environmental resilience.
The related term soil resistance is the inherent capacity to withstand disturbance, while resilience is the capacity to recover after disturbance.
It must be seen against pedogenesis, a process taking thousands of years, compared with the short time humans have depended on and changed soil.
Parent material and topography are passive soil-forming factors, while climate and the biosphere are active; variations in the active factors amount to environmental change or shock.
Soils have endured an oxygen-free atmosphere, the arrival of land plants 420 million years ago and, since the last ice age, extended wet, dry and fire periods.
Open questions are whether soil should stay constant or reach a new equilibrium, and how long it can hold out or adjust on pedological time.
Resilience is limited by the rate and extent of human-imposed change compared with the time soil needs to recover.
In Australia, little more than 200 years of European-style farming has brought salinity, acidity, nutrient decline, erosion and structural decline.

definition.text: Creating new soil and restoring soil health by minimizing topsoil loss, retaining more carbon than is lost, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working.

facts.text: It is a form of ecological regeneration within restoration ecology, reforming degraded soil through biological, chemical or physical processes.
Its benefits include carbon sequestration against climate change, lower erosion risk and greater overall soil resilience.
Healthy soil is a mix of living organisms, organic matter and inorganic material, with air and water typically making up half its volume.
Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by rhizosphere microbes, a symbiosis that maintains mostly fungal living biomass and raises soil carbon.
For optimal plant growth a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 20–30:1 must be maintained.
Soil biodiversity creates competitive pressure that shrinks the niche open to disease and parasitic organisms.
Organic carbon content is one of the most predictable ways to tell whether a soil has degraded.
Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon concentrations, allowing the soil to regenerate.

title: Forms of soil degradation

definition.text: The four general ways soil declines in condition under poor management: erosion, and physical, chemical and biological degradation.

facts.text: Erosion displaces soil by water runoff or wind, typically from bare fields; physical degradation changes structure so water and air cannot enter, as in compaction by large vehicles.
Chemical degradation includes contamination with heavy metals or hydrocarbons, acidification, salinization, nutrient leaching and toxins from mining and waste management.
Biological degradation is a loss of biological activity, as when fertilizer buildup inhibits nitrogen-fixing microbes, bringing biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions and less carbon storage.
One third of the globe's land has degraded soil, with around 500 million hectares degraded in the tropics and subtropics.
Excessive tillage, especially ploughing, leaves soil open to wind erosion, and farm vehicles compact it, reducing its permeability to air and water.
Chemical fertilizer suppresses nitrogen-fixing microbes and raises nitrous oxide emissions; replacing lost fertility with more fertilizer creates a positive feedback loop.
Overgrazing removes plant roots, reducing organic content and the symbiosis between plants and the soil microbiome.
Urban construction compacts and seals soils, intensifying storm runoff and erosion, and cities concentrate pollutants that leach into soils.

notes: The one-third share of land with degraded soil (S:66b5eae34558) is another share-of-land estimate; see Global extent of land degradation in degradation-and-desertification.

title: Agricultural soil carbon loss
article: Soil regeneration#Climate change and the carbon cycle

definition.text: The release of soil carbon to the atmosphere through farming and fossil fuel use, which regenerative practices aim to reverse.

facts.text: Some 61 billion tonnes of carbon leave soils each year through decomposition and oxidation of organic carbon, and a similar amount returns through decomposition and plant–microbe symbiosis.
The top two meters of soil hold an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes of carbon, more than the atmosphere (879 billion) and vegetation (600 billion) together.
Since farming began, an estimated 133 billion tonnes of carbon has been lost from soil, mostly in the last two centuries of mechanised agriculture.
Cutting soil emissions reduces overall greenhouse gas emissions, and regenerative practices can act as natural carbon dioxide removal.

title: Regenerative soil practices

definition.text: Farming and management methods, many from conservation agriculture, that regenerate soil and improve its quality.

facts.text: Monoculture depletes soil carbon and nutrients, because each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients.
Cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced soil disturbance, mulch retention and integrated nutrient management increase carbon sequestration and cut fossil fuel use.
Permaculture mimics natural ecosystems with mixed, native and perennial crops and avoids tilling, allowing more sustained contact between soil microbes and roots.
Holistic management, from Allan Savory's work, claims planned grazing can improve soil health and reverse desertification; researchers dispute the desertification claim.
Soil amendments, chosen to suit current soil conditions, sequester toxins, balance pH, add nutrients and promote organisms.

Inorganic amendments improve texture and structure, balance pH and limit heavy-metal availability: alkaline ones include wood ash, ground limestone and red mud, mineral ones gypsum and dredged materials.
Organic amendments such as mulch, compost, biochar, manure and biosolids improve biological activity, water permeability and structure; biosolids are nutrient-rich, so they should be used sparingly.

contested_note: Researchers dispute the claim that holistic planned grazing reverses desertification.

definition.text: The policies, strategies and decision-making processes that nation states and local governments apply to the use of soil.

facts.text: Globally it has been limited to an agricultural perspective because of food insecurity in the most populated regions; in the developing world it favours sustainable agriculture and food security.
It differs from soil management, the practices used to raise and maintain soil fertility, structure and carbon sequestration.

It needs collaboration among governments, local authorities, industries and citizens on coherent policies that regulate soil use, avoid conflicts between users and promote sustainable land management.
Concern over farming's effects such as erosion built awareness of soil governance and made science and technology the link between management and governance.
It usually sits within land governance, with little attention to urban and industrial soils, especially in rapidly urbanizing developing countries.
Global soil governance focuses on degradation's effects on food production and on conflict between space for settlements and for farming.
FAO and UNESCO made a global soil map in 1981; a new global soil map, led by ISRIC with GIS and remote sensing, is being built by a scientific consortium.
The International Union of Soil Sciences proposed 5 December as World Soil Day in 2002, and the UN General Assembly designated it in December 2013.

definition.text: A partnership set up by the FAO and its members in December 2012 to improve governance of the planet's limited soil resources for food security and ecosystem services.

facts.text: Its goal is food security and restored ecosystem services through conserving, enhancing and restoring soils by productive, sustainable use.

It is an open, voluntary partnership of FAO member countries with universities, research centres, soil science societies, UN agencies, NGOs, companies, farmer associations and donors, working through Regional Soil Partnerships.
Its First Plenary Assembly, at FAO headquarters in June 2013, adopted rules of procedure and established the Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils.
The panel's 27 soil experts, representing all regions, advise the partnership on science and advocate sustainable soil management.

conflicts.text: The Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils was established in 2003.
conflicts.note: S:5fedbc8cc783 says the panel was nominated and established at the First Plenary Assembly in June 2013.

definition.text: The European Union's approach to soil, which it treats as a non-renewable resource while leaving its governance largely to member states.

facts.text: In 2006 the European Commission proposed a soil protection framework to unify rules scattered across EU legislation.
Member states rejected it under the subsidiarity principle, arguing their own strong domestic soil policies sufficed, so the EU has no cohesive soil governance policy.
Healthy soils are part of the European Green Deal, and the EU Soil Strategy for 2030, launched in 2021, aims at healthy soils for food security and climate mitigation.
The strategy frames a Soil Monitoring Law, first meant to be legally binding on soil health, whose final version set no obligatory targets and covers only monitoring.

title: Soil governance in India

definition.text: India's policies on soil, shaped by the weight of agriculture in its economy and by widespread farmland degradation.

facts.text: In 2010 agriculture employed 58.2% of India's workforce and contributed 15.7% of GDP.
Excessive, miscalculated fertiliser use aimed at higher output has left nearly two-thirds of India's farmland classed as degraded or sick.
Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006, which tests farmers' soil and advises on fertilizer and crops, was later extended nationally under the Ministry of Agriculture.

India's National Programme to Combat Desertification builds capacity in soil and water management, micro-credit for women and marginalised groups, alternative energy and land legislation for industry and mining.

notes: S:08cb3205d35d says India ratified the UNCCD in 1984, but the Convention was adopted in 1994 (S:859b0116a0fd), so the year is likely wrong and is left out.

title: Urban and industrial soil governance
article: Soil governance#Impacts of industrialization and urbanization

definition.text: Governing soils in cities and industrial areas, where industrialization and urbanization are emerging as major causes of soil degradation, especially in the developing world.

facts.text: Industry alters soil chemistry with heavy metals and effluents, while construction and landfills compact and excavate soil, disturbing water purification and storage.

Poor knowledge of soil management and disregard for the environment drive urban soil degradation, and developing countries often lack resources to enforce policies, leaving soil and water heavily polluted.
Urban soil management uses an interdisciplinary approach to protect soil-dependent biodiversity, reduce industrial pollution and make soil more resilient to construction compaction.
In Central Europe an urban soil management strategy, built on networks of universities and municipal authorities, designs soil strategies for selected cities.

title: Soil bioengineering

definition.text: The use of living plant materials, such as seeds, plants and plant communities, to perform engineering functions like stabilizing slopes and controlling erosion.

facts.text: A discipline of civil engineering, it can sometimes replace classical engineering works but in most cases usefully complements them.
Used for many centuries and promoted with European examples by Schiechtl (1980), it is now practised worldwide on eroding and unstable slopes and embankments.
It works wherever its plants grow well, as in tropical, subtropical and temperate zones, and is limited in arid, frost, alpine and arctic regions and in species-poor areas.
Technically, plantings shield soil from wind, rain, frost and flowing water, slow flow along banks, bind soil, trap snow, sand and sediment, and roughen slopes against avalanches.
Ecologically, they improve the water regime, loosen soil with roots, even out temperatures, enrich nutrients on raw soils and raise yields on neighbouring cropland.
They heal landscapes scarred by landslides, wildfires, mining and construction, and fit structures into the landscape.

Such works are not always cheaper to build, but counting service and maintenance over their lifetime they are normally more economical, since they become living systems that maintain themselves by succession.

notes: The Economic effects section both says the works are not always cheaper to build (S:1e705cf1b0bd) and lists lower construction costs (S:c8f3bc40f80e); the fact follows the first.

definition.text: A subsurface wastewater disposal facility, also called a leach field, that removes contaminants from the liquid leaving a septic tank after anaerobic digestion.

facts.text: A microbial ecosystem breaks down the organic materials in the liquid; the drain field, septic tank and piping together make up a septic system.
It typically has trenches of perforated pipe and porous material, often gravel, covered with soil to keep animals and surface runoff away from the wastewater.
Design is both hydraulic, for the volume of wastewater, and catabolic, for its long-term biochemical oxygen demand.
Just as the septic tank is sized for anaerobic organisms, the field is sized to support aerobic soil microbes that turn the tank's anaerobic effluent into aerobic water.
A biofilm on the trench walls uses atmospheric oxygen to break down organic compounds; incompletely oxidized effluent shows as hydrogen sulfide odors or iron bacteria in nearby wells.
Its microbes can barely break down petroleum products and chlorinated solvents and cannot remove dissolved metals, and bleach or sanitizers can slow or stop their activity.
A field with several disposal areas lets one rest while nematodes eat accumulated biofilm and fats, easing bioclogging, though percolation rarely regains its original clean-water rate.
Adding a biofilter lowers the effluent's oxygen demand, though not its volume, so the field can be smaller and more land is left free.

definition.text: Judging whether a soil can receive septic tank effluent, by a percolation test or by reading the soil's morphology.

facts.text: The soil must be permeable enough for effluent to percolate away yet fine enough to hold back pathogenic bacteria and viruses; percolation tests time clean water dispersing from a trench.
Aerobic conditions must kill pathogens before they reach wells or surface water: sand and gravel pass wastewater too fast, while silt and clay filter pathogens but limit flow.
Where seasonal high water tables limit sizing, a soil scientist reads texture, structure, consistency, pore and root distribution, and the colour signatures of water-table fluctuation.
In service, percolation falls as microbial biofilm, fine particles, congealed fats, rising groundwater and frozen ground clog or limit the trench's soil interface.

title: Soil Health Card Scheme

definition.text: An Indian government scheme, launched on 19 February 2015, that gives farmers soil cards with crop-wise nutrient and fertiliser recommendations based on soil tests.

facts.text: It promotes soil-test-based, balanced fertiliser use so farmers get higher yields at lower cost; experts identify the soil's micronutrient deficiencies and suggest remedies.
The government allocated ₹568 crore (US$61 million), and the 2016 Union budget gave states ₹100 crore (US$11 million) to make cards and set up labs.
By July 2015 only 34 lakh cards had been issued against a 2015–16 target of 84 lakh; by 16 May 2017, 725 lakh cards had been distributed.
Its national form followed Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006, which was credited with helping the state's farm growth reach three times the national rate in 2009.

conflicts.text: The 2015–16 target was 104 lakh soil samples.
conflicts.note: S:ffa6e198594b gives a 2015–16 target of 100 lakh soil samples.

notes: The lead's targets of cards for 14 crore farmers (S:42e718694a49) and results shown on the cards (S:df7d2dde1a18) carry citation-needed tags and are left out.

definition.text: Returning damaged land to some degree of its former state after industry, natural disasters or other harm.

facts.text: Mining, farming and forestry often degrade land; in parts of the United States, reclamation means returning disturbed land to an improved state.
Mine rehabilitation contours waste dumps against erosion, caps sulfide ore with clay to stop acid forming, and covers landfills and tailings with topsoil or soil and vegetation.
Australian mine rehabilitation bonds total $9.49 billion, and reclaiming abandoned US mines is estimated to cost $9.6bn.

definition.text: An underground concrete, fibreglass or plastic chamber where household sewage settles and is anaerobically digested as primary treatment.

facts.text: Solids settle and are digested in the first chamber; the liquid then goes to a septic drain field, which needs a percolation test to show the soil is porous enough.
Sludge builds up faster than it decomposes, so it is pumped out by vacuum truck, every few years in some systems and every 10-20 years in others.
Tanks remove little nitrogen; soils usually retain the phosphorus, but sandy soils near water can become saturated with phosphate and pass it on, risking eutrophication.
About 20 percent of US households relied on septic tanks in 2008, but dense development can push groundwater pollution beyond acceptable limits.

definition.text: Modifying mined land to restore it to an ecologically functional or economically usable state.

facts.text: In open-cut mines, rock backfills the pit, stored pre-mining soil goes on top, then topsoil, and finally vegetation is restored.
The original landscape cannot always be restored; usually the limit is the physical and chemical stabilization of mine waste.
The Forestry Reclamation Approach calls for a loosely graded, uncompacted rooting medium at least four feet deep of topsoil or weathered sandstone.
Under the US Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, operators file a reclamation plan and a bond before mining; a coal tax funds abandoned-mine reclamation.

title: Permaculture

definition.text: An approach to land management and settlement design that copies arrangements seen in flourishing natural ecosystems.

facts.text: Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term in 1978; its three ethics and Holmgren's twelve design principles are widely cited.
Common practices include Hügelkultur (burying wood to hold soil water), sheet mulching, no-till gardening, keyline design and vermicomposting.
It has been largely isolated from science and criticised as pseudo-scientific or poorly defined.
Some 21st-century studies support claims that it improves soil quality and biodiversity; a 2024 review said it strongly enhances carbon stocks and soil quality.

contested_note: Critics call it pseudo-scientific and ill-defined, while recent studies report gains in soil quality and carbon.

definition.text: The many benefits that people derive from ecosystems, such as clean water, food, decomposition of wastes and flood control.

facts.text: The UN Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularized four categories: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services.
Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, make possible others such as food supply, flood regulation and water purification.
Regulating services include waste decomposition and detoxification, and erosion regulation affects people indirectly through environmental conditions.

New York City restored its Catskill watershed, where soil absorption and filtration, roots and soil microbes brought water back to standard, for $1–1.5 billion instead of a $6–8 billion filtration plant.
Evaluations of ecosystem services may assign them an economic value.

title: Active carbon

definition.text: A newer soil health measurement of active carbon, the most readily usable portion of a soil's total organic carbon.

facts.text: Active carbon contributes greatly to the functioning of the soil food web.
It joins established soil health measures such as microbial biomass and activity, enzymes, soil organic matter, total nitrogen, available nutrients, porosity, aggregate stability and compaction.

notes: The phrase dossier also listed 'permanganate oxidizable carbon' (POXC), but no crawled sentence names the permanganate method; the entry is limited to what the urban agriculture page says.

definition.text: A wastewater system that treats and disposes of effluent on the property that produces it, where there is no public sewer.

facts.text: Most are conventional: a septic tank plus a subsurface infiltration system; such systems handle about 25% of domestic wastewater in the US.
Decomposition by natural organisms remains the main disposal mechanism, so minimum retention times and distances to surface water and wells are set.
Site evaluation characterizes soils, slopes and local hydrology and geology to set the design and placement of system components.
Septic systems are the third most common source of groundwater pollution in the US, failing through poor siting, design or maintenance.
